reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use among educational services firms, NAICS 61, at 30.0% in the latest period, measured as the share answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks. The prior period was 35.5%. The question was first asked in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material.

The Department of Education's AI guidance page shows what deployment looks like inside a federal education agency. ED has assembled an inventory of AI use cases, and the listed tools include CAISY, described as enhancing decision-making and operational efficiency through real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation, Grammarly's AI assistant for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration, and AWS Bedrock for building and scaling applications powered by foundation models. Other listed uses include generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating code snippets including R code for data analysis, converting data types such as a county name into its FIPS code, generating mock data sets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and suggesting descriptive paragraphs and qualifications for public positions.

On where vendors and money concentrate, the ED inventory names commercial tools, Grammarly, Otter.AI, and AWS Bedrock, alongside an internal system, CAISY. HolonIQ is described as the market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning, and its page describes sizing addressable markets, forecasting scenarios, and mapping competitors and partners. The excerpt carries no education-specific figures, so nothing here quantifies that market.

This site's own catalog lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The catalog does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

The sources report no ROI figures for education. ED describes CAISY as helping organizations reduce costs, boost productivity, and make more accurate, data-driven decisions, and describes other tools as saving time, improving accessibility, and streamlining content creation, but these are statements of intended benefit rather than measured returns.

On risk and regulatory posture, ED's guidance frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education, and its OCIO supports the Department's adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement under the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. One listed use case feeds fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to ensure proper filters and data loss prevention are in place. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the measured adoption figure is 30.0% against a prior period of 35.5%, the documented uses are largely administrative, drafting, and analysis tasks rather than instruction, and the material here offers no cost or outcome data to support a deployment case.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
